Lalleśvarī
------------------------------------------
India has produced quite a good number of man-saints whose extra-ordinary spiritual wisdom or devotion to God was unparallelled. However, equally great have been the women-saints though their number was comparatively less.
One such, a gem among them, was लल्लेश्वरी of Kashmir. Lallā, Lallā Ded, Lāl Ded and Lallayogīśvarī were the other names by which she was known. She lived in the 14th century A. D.
She was born in the family of Kashmiri Paṇḍits belonging to the Śaiva tradition, in the town of Paṇḍrentān (or Purāṇādhiṣṭhāna) near Srinagar. At the age of twelve, she was married to Nicābāt of Pampāpura (or Padmāpura). She was renamed as पद्मावती by her ड़थेर्- in-law.
Though her मोथेर्-in-law was harassing her severely, she silently put up with it for a long period of twelve years. However, finding it impossible to bear it any more, she abandoned the होउसे and the family, and started roaming about like a mendicant, in search of शिव, her Lord.
Fortunately, in her wanderings, she succeeded in getting a great गुरु (spiritual teacher) known as Siddhanātha. Under his guidance, she became an adept in योग and spiritual wisdom. After thus attaining perfection, she resumed her peripatetic life during which period many persons became her disciples or followers. She also met many saṁnyāsins (monks) and Muslim Fakirs (holy-men) with whom she used to hold discussions. It is said that she could remember her previous lives and also had many yogic powers.
During such wanderings she would often go into ecstacy, dance and sing songs on her Lord शिव. Quite a few of these compositions—all in the Kashmiri language—have been preserved. Some of them have also been published with English translation. Though they are apparently couched in a simple language, they are pregnant with high philosophical content.
Nothing is known about her final days and demise.
As regards her teachings contained in her songs, admirable service has been done by one paṇḍit, भास्कराचार्य by name, who has rendered them in Sanskrit, in sixty beautiful verses.
Her struggles towards perfection passed through several stages. In the first stage, she had several questions to ask, several doubts to be cleared. Some of them are:
I do not know from where I came and to where I go. Yet, the desire to know Him is sustaining me.
O गुरु! Please teach me that which will enlighten me.
Wandering around the places of पिल्ग्रिमगे or praising Him through songs did not help me much. Finally I discovered Him in myself.
In the second stage she acquired the knowledge of the scriptures. She discovered that Māyā (cosmic illusory power) binds whereas true knowledge liberates.
In the third stage she concentrated on sādhanās or spiritual practices. She discovered that:
Mind is responsible for bondage and लिबेरतिओन्.
One should be controlled in eating as also other enjoyments.
Prāṇāyāma (breath-control) helps in controlling the मिन्द्, as also mauna (observing silence).
Real worship of God is accomplished by meditation rather than by external rituals.
In the fourth stage she refers to her spiritual experiences. She attained equanimity of मिन्द् and realised the importance of प्रणव or Om.
In the fifth or the last stage, she describes as to how she lived as a free bird after realising her Lord शिव, inside herself. She had totally transcended the six evils like lust and anger.
Her philosophy of life was what is now known as Kashmir शैविस्म्.

Lalitā
------------------------------------------
An aspect of the देवी which is more widely worshipped in South India is ललिता त्रिपुरसुन्दरी. Repetition of the well-known Lalitāsahasranāma and Triśatī ललिता देवी.">1, as also the worship of her emblem, the ‘Śrīcakra,’ are extremely popular. The initiation into her powerful मन्त्र, the pañcadaśākṣarī (mantra of 15 letters) is an esoteric rite. Regular worship of the श्रीचक्र is said to yield any result the devotee desires.
If दुर्गा and Kālī represent the aspects of power of the Goddess, ललिता represents the aspect of beauty. Hence her form is depicted as extremely beautiful and her worship more refined.
According to the Lalitopākhyāna of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, ललिता देवी manifested herself in the midst of a disc of extreme brilliance, that arose from the sacrificial pit when इन्द्र was performing a sacrifice in honour of her. At the behest of the gods assembled there, she chose to wed कामेश्वर (Lord शिव). She destroyed the demon भण्डासुर and annihilated his city, the Śoṇitapura. Viśvakarmā, the engineer of the gods, built a gorgeous city ‘Śrīpura’ on the mountain मेरु, for her sake, where, along with her spouse शिव कामेश्वर, she is residing eternally. The श्रीचक्र actually represents the देवी in this Śrīpura.
Bhaṇḍāsura, the shameless demon, living in the Śoṇitapura, the city of blood and flesh, is actually the ego which makes the सोउल् identify itself with the body and estrange itself from all the divine forces. When the देवी, who is the embodiment of God’s power and grace, ‘kills’ it, she is actually liberating it from its stifling limitations.
Lalitā is usually depicted as slightly red in colour (as that of the dawn) and extraordinarily beautiful. In her four hands she is holding a bow of sugarcane, arrows, the goad (aṅkuśa) and the noose (pāśa). Sometimes she is shown holding a wine cup made of diamond. One of her feet, usually the left, is shown resting on a pedestal, also of diamond.
The bow made of sugarcane actually represents the मिन्द्. It is through the मिन्द् that we experience all joy. Hence it is described as made of sugarcane. The bow is the instrument for discharging the arrows. The मिन्द् is the instrument by which the sense organs are ‘shot’ towards the sense-objects. Hence it is described as a bow. The arrows are the pañca-तन्मात्रस्, the five subtle elements of आकाश (ether), वायु (air), अग्नि (fire), āpas (water), पृथ्वी (earth). The sense organs like the eye and the ear, are products of these subtle elements and are discharged like arrows, through the मिन्द्, towards the sense-objects. Hence the subtle elements are described as the arrows in her hand. She is the power that energises and controls our minds and sense organs. This is the underlying idea. The पाश (noose) is actually राग (attachment) which binds. The aṅkuśa (goad) is krodha (anger, aversion) which hurts. The power that animates our attachments and aversions is also hers. If we forget her, she can bind us with rāgapāśa, and pierce us with the krodhāṅkuśa. If we take refuge in her, she can withdraw them into her hands and thereby free us from their torment.
An account of ललिता cannot be complete without a few words of description of the श्रीचक्र. The श्रीचक्र is essentially a यन्त्र. यन्त्र, a two-dimensional or geometric pattern which can be drawn; and (c) the मन्त्र, the sound form or the thought form, which can be uttered in contemplation. The `mūrti' is usually described in the appropriate dhyānaśloka (verse chanted at the beginning of meditation, to call up the form of the deity into the मिन्द्) and dealt with in greater detail in the iconographical works. The यन्त्र and मन्त्र are described in tāntric works. The मन्त्र, when received from a competent गुरु and repeated with intense faith and devotion, is capable of revealing the form of the deity by setting up appropriate vibrations in the आकाश (ether) which pervades everything including one's own body and मिन्द्. The यन्त्र, the geometrical abode of the deity, when drawn properly (using the dot, the straight line, the triangle, the circle, the segment and so on), and installed, gets charged as it were, binding the contemplated deity to itself. Though the श्रीचक्र is comparatively more well-known, there are a good number of other yantras or चक्रस् which are still very much in vogue.">2 The form and pattern of the deity. It is a rather complicated geometrical figure of forty three triangles formed by the intersection of nine triangles, of which five have their apexes downward and the other four upward. This is surrounded by concentric circles with eight and then sixteen lotus petals. The whole figure is skirted by a square of three lines with openings in the middle of each side. There is a dot in the centre of the entire diagram.
This dot represents the combination of शिव and शक्ति, as also the first throb, which gradually gathers momentum and gets concentrated into a polarisation of शिव and शक्ति, but continuing to keep the original शिव-शक्ति combination also. The process repeats continuously resulting in various levels of च्रेअतिओन्, which are depicted by the different triangles and the lotus petals.
The श्रीचक्र can be used for permanent worship either in the form of a यन्त्र (two dimensional engraved figure) or in the form of मेरु (three dimensional figure).

Lalitopākhyāna
(‘story related to the [Divine मोथेर्] ललिता’)
------------------------------------------
Lalitā, an aspect of पार्वती is an extremely popular goddess in South India. The two hymns addressed to her, the Lalitāsahasranāma and the Lalitātriśatī, are considered as mantras, the recitation of which can grant the fulfilment of any wish.
They are considered to be a part of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa.
The Lalitopākhyāna is said to be an integral part of this purāṇa and appears in its Uttarakhaṇḍa. It has 32 chapters and 2743 verses.
Cast in the form of a dialogue between हयग्रीव and अगस्त्य, it deals exhaustively with the story of Lalitādevī. This story can be summarised very briefly as follows:
When शिव reduced मन्मथ (Cupid, Eros) to ashes, the same was shaped into a beautiful image by Citra-कर्म, one of the attendants of शिव. By chance, शिव’s eyes fell on this image and lo! it sprang to life. शिव gave this newly born person several boons, a life of 60,000 years and invincibility during this period. He came to be known as भण्डासुर and started ruling over the देवस् (gods) and the दानवस्. Even इन्द्र, the king of the gods, became subservient to him. By the time his allotted duration of life was over, the gods, under the leadership of इन्द्र, performed a big sacrifice from which Lalitādevī emerged and assured them that she would destroy भण्डासुर and restore their kingdom to them.
As per the desire of the gods including ब्रह्मा, the creator, Lalitādevī was married to शिव (Kāmeśvara) (since actually she was पार्वती in that form). Then the देवी started on her victory expedition against भण्डासुर. After a fierce fight, he as also all his associates, were decimated.
The overjoyed gods prayed to her with a long and beautiful hymn (Ch. 25, verses 10 to 42).
The work ends with the eulogy of the pañcadaśākṣarī मन्त्र, the मन्त्र of 15 letters, which must be received from a competent गुरु or spiritual preceptor.

Lalitātriśatī
(‘[hymn of] three hundred names of ललिता [Divine मोथेर्]’)
------------------------------------------
The sage हयग्रीव was an emanation from god हयग्रीव, an aspect of Lord विष्णु. It was this sage, who was an ardent devotee of the Divine मोथेर् ललिता, that taught the Lalitāsahasranāma स्तोत्र to अगस्त्य. Even after listening to it, the sage अगस्त्य somehow felt that there was some vacuum in his heart, to fill which, he caught hold of the feet of the sage हयग्रीव and entreated him to teach him further. Three years passed by in this way! Then the Divine मोथेर् Lalitādevī herself appeared on the scene and commanded हयग्रीव to teach the Lalitātriśatī hymn also to the sage अगस्त्य. Thereupon, हयग्रीव gladly taught it to him.
As per this story, the Lalitātriśatī is even more powerful in its efficacy than the Lalitāsahasranāma!
The speciality of this hymn of three hundred names of the Divine मोथेर् ललिता is that it contains the famous pañca-daśākṣarī मन्त्र skilfully imbedded.
Hence all the rules that are enunciated for the recitation of the bigger hymn, apply here also.
The text has a pūrvapīṭhikā (prologue) and a phalaśruti (epilogue giving the fruits of recitation).
There is a well-known commentary on this hymn attributed to शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) though the scholars are not unanimous about his being the original (or Ādi-) शङ्कर.
See also LALITĀSAHASRANĀMA.

Lāldāsīs
(‘followers of Lāldās’)
------------------------------------------
One of the religious sects thrown up by the भक्ति Movement is that of Lāldās who lived in the latter half of the 16th century (d. A. D. 1647). He belonged to the Meo caste (robbers by profession!) and was born in Alwar of Rajasthan. He was deeply influenced by कबीर् (A. D. 1440-1518) and Dādu (A. D. 1544-1603). His sayings and songs, composed as a work, are known as ‘Bānī’.
Lāldāsīs are his followers. They lay great stress on the repetition of Rāmnām (Lord राम’s name) as the only sādhana or spiritual practice.

Lalitāsahasranāma
(‘one thousand names of [the Divine मोथेर्] ललिता’)
------------------------------------------
The Sanskrit स्तोत्र literature (hymnology) in हिन्दुइस्म् is very vast. Some varieties of stotras are considered as very powerful, like mantras or mystical formulae. Their chanting, either ceremonially or even simply—but with faith and devotion—is said to confer on the votaries whatever they want. The sahasranāma (one thousand names) stotras belong to this group.
The Lalitāsahasranāma is one such, which is not only famous but also popular even today, especially in South India. Actually, it forms the 36th chapter of the work Lalitopākhyāna which itself, again, is a part of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa.
It was taught by the sage हयग्रीव (an emanation of the हयग्रीव इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) to the sage अगस्त्य at the latter’s earnest entreaties.
This wonderful and powerful hymn was composed by the Vāgdevatās or the goddesses presiding over the power of speech, like Vaśinī and her companions after being commanded by the देवी herself.
The thousand names beginning with the word ‘Śrīmātā’ and ending with the word ‘Lalitāmbikā’ and spread over 183 ślokas or verses reflect an infinite variety of the Divine मोथेर् ललिता’s beauties, splendours, powers and doings. Many of the names are highly esoteric in nature and are difficult to comprehend without the help of a teacher who is an adept in the science called Śrīvidyā (See ŚRĪVIDYĀ.).
The ceremonial recitation is generally accompanied by the worship of the श्रीचक्र (See ŚRĪCAKRA for details.) with बिल्व leaves (Aegle marmelos) or तुलसी leaves (holy basil) and repetition of the pañcadaśākṣarīmantra (mantra of 15 syllables or letters). The chanting can also be done without these formalities.
The phalaśruti (that part of the hymn which narrates the fruits of the recitation) gives a long list of the benefits that a votary who chants it with due respect and faith, gets. This list includes such results as the merit equal to that of establishing millions of Śivaliṅgas at काशी, destruction of the effects of even the most heinous sins, the merit of performing numberless अश्वमेध sacrifices and so on.
There are five commentaries on this text. Out of these, the Saubhāgya Bhāskara of Bhāskararāya (also known as Bhāsurānandanātha) is considered the best.
See BHĀSKARARĀYA.
